titleEn: Autonomous spraying cuts chemical use by 85% at Coggan Farms
titleZh: 自主喷洒机器人使Coggan农场化学品用量减少85%
summaryZh: 澳大利亚Coggan农场自2021年起部署两台SwarmFarm自主喷洒机器人，配备Weed-It光学点喷摄像头和AutoFill自动加药系统，在休耕期除草作业中实现约85%的化学品节省，部分场景高达95%。该案例展示了自主机器人如何应对劳动力短缺、降低投入成本并提升作业一致性，为大型种植与养殖混合农场提供了可量化的投资回报参考。
featuredReason: 该案例以详实的成本数据和投资回报分析，展示了自主喷洒机器人在大型混合农场中减少85%化学品用量的实际效果，对关注农业自动化、精准植保和劳动力替代的智慧畜牧从业者具有重要参考价值。
contentFull:
Autonomous spraying cuts chemical use by 85% at Coggan Farms

 28-09 | Smart farming | Article

LinkedInFacebookXWhatsAppPrint

Tom, Sarah and Phillip Coggan. The family uses autonomous SwarmFarm Robotics sprayers for targeted weed control, reducing chemical use during fallow spraying. Photos: Chris McCullough

Labour shortages and rising machinery costs prompted Australian mixed farmer Tom Coggan to invest in autonomous spraying. Coggan Farms now operates 2 SwarmFarm Robotics SwarmBots equipped with Weed-It spot-spraying cameras and AutoFill technology. During fallow spraying, the farm typically saves around 85% on chemical use.

Coggan Farms has been operating 2 autonomous SwarmBots since 2021 and 2022 respectively. The machines are mainly used for weed control on fallow land, where targeted spraying has significantly reduced chemical use. The business later added SwarmFarm Robotics’ AutoFill technology, allowing the machines to refill their spray tanks automatically and further reducing the amount of labour required.

Coggan Farms covers more than 65,000 acres near Meandarra in Queensland, Australia.Spread across more than 65,000 acres near Meandarra in Queensland, Australia, Coggan Farms combines crop production with livestock farming. The business is run by Phillip and Cindy Coggan together with their children Emily, Tom and Sarah. Tom Coggan is the fifth generation of the family to farm there and has been closely involved in introducing robotic technology to the business. “Our business includes cattle and lamb feedlots, irrigated and dryland farming, extensive grazing country and a Meatmaster Stud operation,” he says. “The properties have been family-owned and operated since 1937, with multiple generations involved in the business. Around 32,000 acres is used for our cropping programme, growing barley, wheat, chickpeas, canola, sorghum and forage sorghum. Our crop rotations are designed and changed to suit seasonal conditions. Yield averages vary significantly depending on rainfall and those conditions.”

The decision to go for robots was driven by ongoing staff shortages, increasing equipment and operational costs

Labour shortages drive automation

Operating such a large area requires considerable labour. As recruiting staff became increasingly difficult, the family started looking for ways to automate some of its fieldwork. “The decision to go for robots was driven by ongoing staff shortages, increasing equipment and operational costs, and the need to consistently repeat weed-control operations with high accuracy and efficiency,” Coggan says.

Before the autonomous machines arrived, weed control was carried out using operator-driven tractors fitted with camera-based spraying systems. “The first robot, the SB032 called Delta 2, arrived in December 2021 and the second, the SB036 called Hotel 2, came in 2022. We later invested in the AutoFill technology in 2025.”

The 2 robots are predominantly used in the cropping operation, particularly during fallow periods when repeated and targeted weed control is required. Their ability to work for extended periods also reduces the need for additional operators. “Our robots are SB032 and SB036 from the SwarmBot 5 platform. Each machine is fitted with an 18-metre Hayes boom and Weed-It optical spot-spray cameras, along with a 3,000-litre spray tank,” Coggan says. “The machines are powered by approximately 75hp diesel engines and generally require refuelling every 24 to 30 hours of operation, depending on conditions and workload.”

Targeted spraying has produced some of the largest savings. “The biggest advantage for us has been chemical savings through targeted spot spraying. In some situations, we have achieved reductions of up to 95% in chemical usage, although typical savings average around 85%.”

The AutoFill system allows the SwarmBots to refill their spray tanks automatically before returning to work, reducing operator involvement and downtime.Learning to work with robots

Introducing autonomous machinery required changes to existing working practices, particularly during the initial implementation period. “There was definitely a learning curve initially, particularly around integrating the technology into daily farm operations and adapting existing workflows,” Coggan says.

“However, once the systems were established and staff became familiar with the platform, the setup and day-to-day operation became straightforward. The support from SwarmFarm during implementation and training was also very valuable in helping with the transition.”

AutoFill reduces operator involvement

Coggan Farms added SwarmFarm Robotics’ AutoFill system in 2025. The autonomous docking and chemical-handling system allows a SwarmBot to return to a filling station, refill its spray tank and resume work without an operator carrying out the process manually. The system can store, measure and mix multiple chemicals, flush valves and record each fill. “The AutoFill system has been a major advantage from both a labour and efficiency perspective,” Coggan says. “It allows the robots to refill and return to work with minimal operator involvement, which reduces downtime and keeps the machines operating for longer periods. “From a logistics standpoint, it has simplified chemical handling and improved workflow around spray operations. Instead of constantly moving people and machinery around paddocks, the robots can operate more independently while staff focus on other jobs around the farm. “It also improves consistency and accuracy in chemical mixing and loading.”

Each SwarmBot at Coggan Farms is fitted with an 18-metre Hayes boom, Weed-It optical spot-spray cameras and a 3,000-litre spray tank.Consistency over long working hours

Coggan sees consistency as another important benefit of autonomous spraying, particularly across large areas. “One of the biggest benefits that is sometimes overlooked is consistency,” he says. “The robots are able to repeatedly carry out operations with the same level of accuracy regardless of time of day or operator fatigue. That consistency becomes extremely valuable during large-scale fallow spraying programmes. Another major factor is scalability. Autonomous systems allow operations to expand spraying capacity without needing to proportionally increase labour, which is becoming increasingly important in agriculture.”

The biggest advantage for us has been chemical savings through targeted spot spraying

Calculating the payback

The initial investment in autonomous machinery is substantial, Coggan acknowledged. However, he said the combination of lower chemical use, labour savings, reduced machinery wear and the ability to make better use of spraying windows has produced positive results for the business. “The payback can vary depending on the season, spray area and chemical prices, but the robots have definitely saved us a lot through reduced chemical use, lower labour needs and better overall efficiency,” he says. “We generally see around 85% chemical savings during fallow spraying, which makes a huge difference to input costs. Being able to keep the machines running for long hours with very little supervision has also helped us get across more country and stay on top of operations when timing matters.”

Autonomous spraying allows farm staff to focus on other work while the SwarmBots carry out weed-control operations.According to SwarmFarm Robotics, a SwarmBot costs about AUD$360,000 (€220,000). Implements such as sprayers, mowers and slashers represent a further investment, while the AutoFill system costs around AUD$80,000 (€50,000). The company says some customers achieve a payback period of 12 to 18 months through savings on chemicals, fuel and labour. Actual payback depends on factors including machine utilisation, input costs and the type of work performed.

Depending on field conditions and workload, the SwarmBots generally require refuelling after 24 to 30 hours of operation.Comparing costs

SwarmFarm Robotics has also developed an online calculator that allows farmers to compare autonomous machinery with conventional self-propelled sprayers or tractor-based systems. Users enter information including farm area and chemical, fuel and labour costs. The tool then calculates annual costs such as capital expenditure, depreciation, repairs, fuel, labour and chemicals for 3 different machinery setups.

The comparison is intended to give farmers an indication of the potential operating-cost differences between conventional and autonomous spraying systems.

The Coggan family can monitor information including operating hours, areas sprayed and spray mixes from mobile devices.LinkedInFacebookXWhatsAppPrint

translationZh:
Tom、Sarah和Phillip Coggan。这个家族使用SwarmFarm Robotics自主喷洒机器人进行靶向除草，在休耕喷洒期间减少了化学品用量。图片来源：Chris McCullough

劳动力短缺和机械成本上升促使澳大利亚混合农场主Tom Coggan投资自主喷洒技术。Coggan农场目前运营着2台SwarmFarm Robotics的SwarmBot机器人，配备了Weed-It点喷摄像头和AutoFill技术。在休耕喷洒期间，该农场通常可节省约85%的化学品用量。

Coggan农场自2021年和2022年起分别运营2台自主SwarmBot机器人。这些机器主要用于休耕地的杂草控制，靶向喷洒显著减少了化学品用量。该农场后来还增加了SwarmFarm Robotics的AutoFill技术，使机器能够自动补充喷药罐，进一步减少了所需劳动力。

Coggan农场位于澳大利亚昆士兰州Meandarra附近，占地面积超过65,000英亩。该农场将作物种植与畜牧养殖相结合，由Phillip和Cindy Coggan及其子女Emily、Tom和Sarah共同经营。Tom Coggan是家族第五代务农者，一直深度参与将机器人技术引入农场运营。他说：“我们的业务包括牛和羔羊育肥场、灌溉和旱作农业、大面积放牧以及一个Meatmaster种畜场。这些产业自1937年以来一直由家族拥有和经营，多代人参与其中。约32,000英亩用于作物种植，种植大麦、小麦、鹰嘴豆、油菜、高粱和饲用高粱。我们的作物轮作根据季节条件进行设计和调整。平均产量因降雨和这些条件而有很大差异。”

**劳动力短缺推动自动化**

经营如此大的面积需要大量劳动力。随着招聘员工变得越来越困难，这个家族开始寻找自动化部分田间作业的方法。Coggan说：“选择机器人的决定是由持续的劳动力短缺、不断增加的设备和运营成本，以及以高精度和高效率持续重复除草作业的需求所驱动的。”

在自主机器到来之前，除草作业使用配备摄像头喷洒系统的有人驾驶拖拉机进行。“第一台机器人SB032，名为Delta 2，于2021年12月到达；第二台SB036，名为Hotel 2，于2022年到达。我们后来在2025年投资了AutoFill技术。”

这2台机器人主要用于作物种植作业，特别是在需要反复进行靶向除草的休耕期。它们能够长时间工作的能力也减少了对额外操作员的需求。Coggan说：“我们的机器人是SwarmBot 5平台的SB032和SB036。每台机器配备18米Hayes喷杆和Weed-It光学点喷摄像头，以及3,000升喷药罐。机器由约75马力的柴油发动机驱动，通常每24至30小时运行需要加油一次，具体取决于条件和工作量。”

靶向喷洒带来了最大的节省。“对我们来说最大的优势是通过靶向点喷实现的化学品节省。在某些情况下，我们实现了高达95%的化学品用量减少，不过典型节省平均在85%左右。”

AutoFill系统允许SwarmBot在返回作业前自动补充喷药罐，减少了操作员参与和停机时间。

**学习与机器人协作**

引入自主机械需要改变现有的工作方式，尤其是在初始实施阶段。Coggan说：“初期肯定有一个学习曲线，特别是在将技术整合到日常农场运营和调整现有工作流程方面。”

“然而，一旦系统建立起来，员工熟悉了平台，设置和日常操作就变得简单了。SwarmFarm在实施和培训方面的支持对帮助过渡也非常宝贵。”

**AutoFill减少操作员参与**

Coggan农场于2025年增加了SwarmFarm Robotics的AutoFill系统。这个自主对接和化学品处理系统允许SwarmBot返回加药站，补充喷药罐并恢复作业，无需操作员手动完成该过程。该系统可以存储、计量和混合多种化学品，冲洗阀门并记录每次加药。Coggan说：“AutoFill系统从劳动力和效率角度来看都是一个重大优势。它允许机器人在最少操作员参与的情况下补充药剂并返回作业，这减少了停机时间并使机器能够运行更长时间。从物流角度来看，它简化了化学品处理并改善了喷洒作业的工作流程。机器人可以更独立地运行，而员工则专注于农场周围的其他工作，而不是不断在田间调动人员和机械。它还提高了化学品混合和装载的一致性和准确性。”

Coggan农场的每台SwarmBot都配备了18米Hayes喷杆、Weed-It光学点喷摄像头和3,000升喷药罐。

**长时间工作的一致性**

Coggan认为一致性是自主喷洒的另一个重要优势，尤其是在大面积作业中。他说：“有时被忽视的最大好处之一是一致性。机器人能够以相同的精度反复执行操作，无论是一天中的什么时间或操作员是否疲劳。在大规模休耕喷洒项目中，这种一致性变得极其有价值。另一个重要因素是可扩展性。自主系统允许在不按比例增加劳动力的情况下扩大喷洒能力，这在农业中变得越来越重要。”

对我们来说最大的优势是通过靶向点喷实现的化学品节省

**计算投资回报**

Coggan承认，自主机械的初始投资是巨大的。然而，他表示，降低的化学品用量、劳动力节省、减少的机械磨损以及更好地利用喷洒窗口期的能力相结合，为农场带来了积极的结果。他说：“投资回报因季节、喷洒面积和化学品价格而异，但机器人确实通过减少化学品用量、降低劳动力需求和更好的整体效率为我们节省了大量资金。我们在休耕喷洒期间通常看到约85%的化学品节省，这对投入成本产生了巨大影响。能够让机器在极少监督下长时间运行，也帮助我们覆盖更多土地，在时机关键时保持作业进度。”

自主喷洒使农场员工能够专注于其他工作，而SwarmBot则执行除草作业。据SwarmFarm Robotics称，一台SwarmBot的价格约为36万澳元（22万欧元）。喷药器、割草机和碎草机等农具代表额外投资，而AutoFill系统价格约为8万澳元（5万欧元）。该公司表示，一些客户通过化学品、燃料和劳动力节省实现了12至18个月的投资回报期。实际回报取决于机器利用率、投入成本和工作类型等因素。

根据田间条件和工作量，SwarmBot通常每24至30小时运行后需要加油。

**成本比较**

SwarmFarm Robotics还开发了一款在线计算器，允许农民将自主机械与传统的自走式喷药器或拖拉机系统进行比较。用户输入农场面积以及化学品、燃料和劳动力成本等信息。该工具随后计算3种不同机械配置的年度成本，如资本支出、折旧、维修、燃料、劳动力和化学品。

该比较旨在让农民了解传统喷洒系统和自主喷洒系统之间潜在的运营成本差异。

Coggan家族可以通过移动设备监控运行时间、喷洒面积和喷洒混合物等信息。
